paras: The hanging of an army recruit at Livingston, Montana, was an assault in which 'indignant citizens' strung up a recently arrived recruit to make him confess to a theft, reported in a syndicated news item in the fall of 1888. The recruit was made to confess and was not reported killed. Newspapers carried the story as an example of the poor quality of army recruits rather than as news of mob violence.

According to the item, sixteen army recruits had recently arrived at Livingston, which the papers placed in Montana. Most of them were said to have gotten into trouble: six were in the guard house for 'serious offenses', three had deserted, and one had been sent to Fort Benton for court-martial.

Another recruit was accused of stealing a satchel, a gold watch and some money 'from a dead woman' and hiding them. Citizens described as 'indignant' strung him up and made him confess where he had hidden the goods. The item gives no date, no name or race for the recruit, no number of participants, and nothing about the dead woman.
No report of an arrest, an inquiry into the hanging, or a charge over the theft appears in the coverage.

The story survives only as a one-sentence brief that ran in white papers far from Montana, first in the Waco Evening News on 3 October 1888. The San Antonio Daily Light printed it the next day under 'Brief Mention', and the Savannah Morning News ran it on 9 October among its 'Items of Interest', between notes on a mind reader and a gold mine in Ireland. Two Dakota weeklies reprinted it on 11 October and 9 November, the Reporter and Farmer omitting the words 'he had stolen'.

Every version opened with the line that 'Army recruits are not of first quality now-a-days', so the hanging served as the last item in a list of the recruits' misdeeds. The item stated the theft as fact and called the citizens 'indignant', without comment on the hanging itself.

reader.title: Hanging of an army recruit at Livingston, Montana
bases: The only text, one filler item, says 'indignant citizens' strung up a recruit to make him confess to a theft; it reports no killing and no attempt to kill (A1, A2, A3).

The item says the recruit was strung up and 'made to confess', which implies he survived, and it reports no death (A1, A2). The 'indignant citizens' acted without stated authority over an alleged theft, but no one was killed, so the standard definition is not met.
All five copies print one unattributed, undated filler item word for word; no local or independent report was found (A1, A2, A3, A4, A5).

framing.detail: A one-sentence brief in miscellany columns ('Brief Mention', 'Items of Interest') framed as a complaint about the quality of army recruits; the citizens are called 'indignant' and the theft is stated as fact, with no comment on the hanging.

conflicts.note: Spelling variation in reprints of the same item; all place it in Montana.
